votes.refutation: I found nothing that fully refutes it. The fail-soft return is deliberate and documented in the comment at settings.py:73-76, and disabling the toggle during an outage is a reasonable fallback. The only defect is the wrong copy during a temporary stamphog DB outage. The toggle is only disabled when `stamphog_review_inbox_prs` is already off, so a user who already turned it on keeps a working control. Nothing is lost or corrupted, and the state clears on the next successful read. The part about the broad except hiding programming errors is weak: the exception is logged with a traceback, and a persistent bug would show up in error tracking. That makes it a real but minor UX inaccuracy (consider), not a correctness defect.

votes.refutation: This is a deliberate, documented design choice, not a defect. The comment at settings.py:73-76 says the flag is informational only. It says the endpoint must not fail because the Stamphog database behind the circuit breaker is down, and that False is the chosen safe fallback, where the toggle stays disabled until the read recovers. The fallback is not silent: logger.exception at settings.py:80 records the full traceback under a named event, so programming errors still surface in error tracking. The user-facing harm is small and short-lived. The misleading copy appears only while the Stamphog database is down. It also appears only for users who have not already turned the toggle on (CodeReviewScene.tsx:1066), so no saved setting is lost or changed. Once the read recovers, the flag corrects itself on the next GET. What remains is a copy-accuracy preference during an outage plus a request to narrow the except clause, and the comment explicitly rejects narrowing it. That is a style or tradeoff disagreement, not a correctness, security or data-loss bug.

votes.refutation: The trigger can happen in production, but only while the Stamphog product database is down. Even then, the only effect is that a tooltip on a switch the user has not turned on yet gives the wrong reason for a short time. Nothing is lost or saved wrongly, and the user cannot make a wrong change. Already opted-in users keep a working switch (CodeReviewScene.tsx:1066). Turning the switch on would not work during that outage anyway, so keeping it disabled is correct. Only the reason text is imprecise. The code comment at settings.py:73-76 records this as an intended tradeoff, and the logger.exception call makes the failure clear to engineers, so the claim that there is "no signal in logs" is wrong. The idea of narrowing the except clause is a style preference. Letting unknown errors escape would bring back the endpoint-wide 500 that the fail-soft design is meant to prevent. This is a copy tweak for an outage-only case, not a defect.
